title: Interpretations Belong to God
theme: In prison Joseph serves Pharaoh's cupbearer and baker. Both dream troubling dreams, and Joseph, crediting God, interprets them: in three days the cupbearer will be restored and the baker executed. It happens exactly so, but the cupbearer forgets Joseph, who remains in prison two more years.

language.note: Used only in the Joseph story in the Old Testament. Joseph insists interpretation belongs to God, not to human skill. Egypt had professional dream interpreters, but they cannot help prisoners.

A pun at the heart of the chapter. For the cupbearer, Pharaoh will 'lift up your head,' meaning restore you. For the baker, Pharaoh will 'lift up your head from you,' meaning behead you. On Pharaoh's birthday he lifts up both heads, in opposite ways.

Joseph asks the cupbearer to remember him, but he 'did not remember Joseph, but forgot him.' The double statement stresses the failure. Unlike the cupbearer, God does remember his people (8:1; 30:22).
Joseph calls his prison a bor, the same word as the pit his brothers threw him in (37:24). He has gone from one pit to another, though innocent both times.

usage.note: Like Joseph, Daniel tells a pagan king that only God can reveal what dreams mean. Both exiles rise to power through God-given wisdom.

usage.theme: Forgotten by people, remembered by God
usage.note: The cupbearer forgets, but God never forgets his own. The thief on the cross asks Jesus to remember him and receives a promise of paradise.
Rescue and judgment come 'on the third day,' a recurring pattern that reaches its climax in Christ's resurrection.

context.setting: The toledot of Jacob (37:2-50:26). Joseph has been in prison for some time after being falsely accused. The chapter sets up his rise in chapter 41, but first adds two more years of waiting (41:1).

flow.label: Two officials in prison
flow.note: Pharaoh's cupbearer and baker offend him and are put in the same prison, where Joseph is assigned to attend them.

flow.label: Troubled by dreams
flow.note: Both dream on the same night. Joseph notices their sad faces, and when they say no one can interpret, he answers that interpretations belong to God.

flow.label: The cupbearer's dream
flow.note: Three branches, grapes and Pharaoh's cup mean the cupbearer will be restored in three days. Joseph asks him to remember him and tells of his innocence.

flow.label: The baker's dream
flow.note: Three baskets with birds eating the baked goods mean the baker will be executed in three days.

flow.label: Fulfilled and forgotten
flow.note: On Pharaoh's birthday the cupbearer is restored and the baker hanged, as Joseph said. But the cupbearer forgets Joseph.

tier1.note: Two years later the cupbearer remembers his fault and tells Pharaoh how Joseph interpreted their dreams correctly.
Until what he had said came to pass, the word of the LORD tested him.

tier2.note: No wise men can show the king the mystery, but there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries.
Two condemned men beside Jesus, one remembered and given life, as Joseph stands between two officials with opposite fates.
Though others forsake me, the LORD will take me in.
Look to the interests of others; Joseph notices the officials' sadness despite his own suffering.

tier3.note: Remember those in prison, as though in prison with them.
Trusting a faithless man in trouble is like a bad tooth or a lame foot.
A cup given into the hand of the king becomes a cup of the new covenant in Jesus.

voices.name: Derek Kidner
voices.view: Kidner notes that Joseph, though suffering unjustly, still pays attention to others' troubles and gives God the credit for his gift. The cupbearer's forgetfulness tests Joseph's patience but also times his release to God's purposes.

voices.name: Victor Hamilton
voices.work: The Book of Genesis (New International Commentary on the Old Testament)
voices.view: Hamilton highlights the wordplay on 'lifting the head,' showing how the same phrase announces life to one and death to the other. The narrative's precision underlines the reliability of the God-given interpretation.

voices.name: Alistair Begg
voices.view: Begg draws attention to the two forgotten years as part of God's providence. God's delays are not his denials, and Joseph's waiting prepared him for his calling.

translations.kjv: And they said unto him, We have dreamed a dream, and there is no interpreter of it. And Joseph said unto them, Do not interpretations belong to God? tell me them, I pray you.

renderings.text: Do not interpretations belong to God?
Do not interpretations belong to God?

translations.note: The versions agree. Joseph's first words recorded in Egypt about his gift point away from himself to God.

translations.kjv: For indeed I was stolen away out of the land of the Hebrews: and here also have I done nothing that they should put me into the dungeon.

renderings.text: that they should put me into the pit
to deserve being put in a dungeon
that they should put me in the dungeon

translations.note: The ESV's 'pit' keeps the word bor from 37:24, connecting Joseph's two unjust imprisonments. Joseph speaks of being 'stolen' without naming his brothers.

steps.gospel: Joseph, an innocent man numbered with transgressors, stands between two condemned men and announces life to one and death to the other. Jesus hung between two criminals and promised paradise to one who asked to be remembered (Luke 23:42-43). The cupbearer forgot Joseph, but Christ never forgets those who call on him. And just as Pharaoh restored the cupbearer to put the cup in the king's hand, Christ restores sinners to fellowship with the King, offering the cup of the new covenant in his blood.
application: Notice and care for others even in our own suffering.
Give God the credit for any gift or insight we have.
Do not put ultimate hope in people's promises; they may forget, but God will not.
Wait patiently through delays, trusting God's timing.
Remember those who have helped us and those who are suffering in prison.

misapplications.claim: Christians should seek to interpret dreams as Joseph did.
misapplications.correction: Joseph's interpretations were special revelation in God's redemptive plan. Believers today are guided chiefly by Scripture, and the chapter's emphasis is that interpretation belongs to God.

misapplications.claim: Joseph's request to be remembered showed a lack of faith.
misapplications.correction: Using legitimate means to seek justice is not unbelief. Joseph trusted God and also spoke up about his innocence.

contrasts.note: The same phrase brings restoration and death.
Two officials, two opposite fates, both foretold.
Human forgetfulness contrasts with God's faithful remembrance.

features.label: Threes
features.note: Three branches, three baskets and three days structure both dreams and their fulfillment.

features.label: Pharaoh's birthday
features.note: The first birthday celebration mentioned in Scripture becomes a day of restoration and execution.

features.label: Double negative
features.note: Verse 23 says the cupbearer 'did not remember' and 'forgot,' stressing his failure.

features.label: Joseph's compassion
features.note: Joseph asks the officials why their faces are sad (v7), showing care in the midst of his own injustice.

steps.summary: Genesis 40 shows Joseph faithful in prison, attentive to others and giving God the glory for interpreting dreams. God's word through him comes true exactly, but the cupbearer forgets him, and Joseph must wait two more years. The chapter teaches trust in God's timing and in his faithful remembrance when people forget.

metaArc.book: This chapter connects Joseph to Pharaoh's court through the cupbearer, preparing for Joseph's summons in chapter 41. The delay heightens the drama of his sudden rise.
metaArc.redemptive: Promise. God prepares the deliverance of his people through the faithfulness of a suffering servant, a pattern fulfilled in Christ.
